analysis.title: After the US vote
key_insights: Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the US midterms by a wider margin than expected, per projections, ending unified Republican control of Washington.
Senate upsets illustrate the scale of the shift: James Talarico in Texas is the first Democrat elected to the Senate there since 1988, and Adam Hamilton in Kansas is the first since 1932.
Trump remains president while Congress turns Democratic. UBS expects divided government, stronger checks on the White House and more political friction.
Democrats gain influence over administration oversight and over spending and debt negotiations. They could seek to soften health care cuts, including Medicaid, and push for more housing support.

UBS says this is not a policy reversal. The presidential veto limits major fiscal reform, and with Congress resisting some spending cuts and the White House set on keeping tax relief, meaningful fiscal consolidation will be difficult. That sets up contentious 2027 debt ceiling negotiations.

CBO projections from February 2026 put the FY2026 federal deficit at 5.8% of GDP, roughly USD 1.9 trillion. Gross government debt exceeds 120% of GDP and net interest costs are about USD 1 trillion in 2026, more than defense spending.
Large US deficits and heavy Treasury issuance can push global yields up just as European governments need to raise spending on defense, security and infrastructure.

Germany has fiscal headroom, so higher spending can boost its economy. Higher-debt countries find it harder to reconcile security needs with fiscal sustainability. Attention is on France, where the government is struggling to contain the deficit ahead of the April presidential election.

In fixed income, UBS sees quality bonds with intermediate maturities as still offering attractive yields. It urges more caution at the longest maturities, even in a base case where yields decline over the coming year.

The White House keeps considerable room on trade, immigration and foreign policy. Bipartisan support for a competitive stance toward China remains, but dependence on Chinese rare earths argues against new restrictions that could disrupt supply chains.

AI regulation matters because data centers need state and local approvals. Hurdles could raise costs and delay projects, but most investment is expected to continue. UBS estimates global AI investment at around USD 1 trillion this year.
For equities, corporate earnings and AI investment remain supportive, but heavy concentration in technology argues for diversification across sectors.
UBS concludes that earnings, growth, inflation, rates, energy, AI and fiscal sustainability matter more for markets than the political color of Congress.

sector_views.rationale: Earnings and AI investment support equities, but high concentration in technology argues for greater diversification across sectors.
Quality bonds with intermediate maturities continue to offer attractive yields.
More caution is warranted at the longest end of the curve even if yields decline over the coming year.

tension_points.theme: US fiscal consolidation under divided government

tension_points.bear_case: The presidential veto limits major fiscal reform, and the White House wants to preserve tax relief, so meaningful fiscal consolidation will be difficult and the 2027 debt ceiling talks could be contentious.
